utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution, assisted today by our case managers, Alma Imamovic and Francisca Duijvestein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP, everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for General Delic. Our case manager is Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Mr. Witness, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the beginning of your testimony, you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. I just want to warn you and remind you that you are still bound by that declaration. Understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mrkaljevic.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to pick up on a theme we were talking about right at the end of the session yesterday, and I'd like to ask you, sir, how the work product of the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department was integrated into planning for military operations of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Intelligence Department was responsible for presenting to the 3rd Corps Staff all fresh intelligence information that could assist in carrying out their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How, sir, would that intelligence information assist the 3rd Corps Staff in carrying out their tasks?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence would normally provide any information that was available on the enemy along the front line, the enemy's forces, and this was necessary in order to be able to plan certain activities in a timely manner. At the same time, intelligence that was of exceptional importance or priority would be passed along as fast as possible, and this would then signal to our units any need for interventions and made it possible for them to organise their defences along the front line in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the working relationship, Mr. Mrkaljevic, between the Intelligence Department and the Security Department of the 3rd Corps during the time that you were assigned to the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Intelligence Department had a good level of cooperation with the Military Security Department. We would exchange all our information on a daily basis, any information that was relevant to us, the Intelligence Department, or to them, the Military Security Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time, sir, in the summer of 1995 through the end of that year, who was the 3rd Corps assistant commander for Security?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the summer of 1995, it was Mr. Ekrem Halihodzic. After that, Mr. Agan Haseljic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mr. Alan"] was appointed. But that was the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, for the record, the transcript didn't catch the name of the person who was appointed after Mr. Ekrem Halihodzic. Could you repeat his name, please?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Agan Haseljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this time period, sir, when you were in the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department, where was or where were the offices of the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department located?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offices were located in the Command building, on the first floor. You took a flight of stairs up to the first floor, and then this was in the left wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, where was the -- let's start with what you've called the Command building. Where was that building, in what town and location?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Command or, rather, the building that housed the Command of the 3rd Corps was in Zenica. These buildings belonged to the Technoprojekt company, and these were just outside the Zenica ironworks compound. This was gate number 4. That's what we used to call it. It was a gate used to access the Zenica ironworks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was the office of the 3rd Corps commander during this time period, summer 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander's office, first you took the stairs to the first floor, and then just on the right, first door on the right, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, if you know, where was the Security Department of the 3rd Corps in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, the assistant commander for Security of the 3rd Corps or, rather -- you took the stairs up to the first floor, you turned right, and then the last door on the left, that's where his office was. Was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Registrar, Your Honours, I would ask that the witness be allowed to draw a sketch of the first floor, the floor plan of the first floor of the 3rd Corps building, as he's described it, and I believe this can be done electronically on the screen using the electronic pen. So I would ask that the usher assist in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, with this technology, you'll be able to draw directly on the screen in front of you, and I would ask you, sir, if you could please draw a floor plan, to the best of your recollection, of the first floor of the 3rd Corps headquarters building to include the commander's office, the Intelligence Department and the Security Departments.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. What I'm drawing now, I'm trying to get my bearings. This is north, right, in relation to the building. This is a reference point for the gate [marks], and these are the cardinal points [marks]. What I'm drawing right now is the staircase into the building. This one is outside the building [indicates] and this one leads up to the first floor [indicates]. Office number 1, this is the 3rd Corps commander's office. Office number 2, this is where the secretary was. Office number 3, the mess where officers of the 3rd Corps took lunch. Office number 4, the people who worked in the officers' restaurant and other auxiliary staff. This was once you took the staircase up to the first floor on the right, there were the commander's offices and on the left was the restaurant and the restaurant staff. Office number 5, the lavatory. Office number 6, assistant commander for Intelligence, 3rd Corps. Office number 7, office number 7 was the operator and the desk clerk of the 3rd Corps. Office number 8, Department for Intelligence and Reconnaissance. Office number 9, my office, and my officers were there too. Office number 10. Office number 10 was for officers from the electronic surveillance team. Office 11 and office 12, as well as office 13 and 14, officers from the Military Security Department. Last office, number 14, assistant commander of the 3rd Corps' military security. I must say this, though: In this room, up to about midway through 1994, there was the deputy commander, Mr. Dzemal Merdan. When officers left for other duties, Mr. Dzemal Merdan was moved to a ground-floor office, and the location was the same where you see office number 6 on the first floor, but on the ground floor, that was Mr. Dzemal Merdan's office. For a brief while, he served as chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, referring to room 14, "up to about midway through 1994, there was the deputy commander, Mr. Dzemal Merdan," after Mr. Merdan moved to the ground floor, who occupied room number 14?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that moment on, room number 14 was occupied by the assistant commander of the 3rd Corps Military Security. Up to that point in time, between 13 and 14, there was a partition that was built, a smaller room, if you like, and assistant commander for Military Security, from the time the corps was set up and until he eventually moved to room 14, used to be in room number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, sir, what officer occupied room number 6? Who was the -- the name of the person who was in room number 6.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Room number 6 was occupied by Mr. Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And room number 14, after Mr. Merdan moved to the first floor, what was the name of the officer or officers who worked in room 14?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Office number 14 was occupied by the assistant commander for Military Security, Mr. Ekrem Halihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, so that we're absolutely clear, what is the name of the person who occupied room number 1?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Office number 1 was occupied by Mr. Commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, so that we're also clear, sir, can you tell us which rooms or numbers of rooms were occupied by the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, the Intelligence Department was in rooms 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10, but certain adjustments were made later on; no significant ones, though. Certain rooms were made over in order to create even better working conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, again just for purposes of clarity, which room or rooms housed the Security Department of the 3rd Corps in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, the Military Security Department was in the right wing of the building. It was in rooms 11, 12, 13 and 14, as I've pointed out already. There were certain adjustments. Rooms were refurbished. Those rooms that were slightly larger, they would be divided in two in order to create two smaller rooms, but this was just to improve their functional aspect, so the conditions were better then for the officers' work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, again, for purposes of clarity, could you again take the marker and place an "X" near the front entrance of this building? I know you described that as you drew it, but could you please place an"X" near the front door where you would enter the building.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. The entrance was this way [indicates]. I'm putting a little cross right there, so these are the steps that you take to get to the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you also, at the beginning, when you drew the sketch, you placed an arrow with the letter "S." Again, can you indicate which direction the letter "S" refers to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The letter "S" or the arrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The "S" on top of the arrow at the upper right of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What direction does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: North.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you indicate on this sketch where gate 4 that you've referred to, the gate into the Zenica ironworks, is located?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Number 1, the railway passing down the -- or past the north flank of the building of the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir, because we've already marked General Mahmuljin's office as number 1. Could you take the number 1 at the railroad tracks and make that into a number 15, please?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, I can make it over into 15 [marks]. 15 is the railway track passing the northern face of the Corps Command. Number 16 is the fence that was put up to the west of the Corps Command building. Gate number 4 used to access the Zenica ironworks compound, is right here, number 17. This was about 30 metres northwest from the Corps Command building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrkaljevic. I would ask the sketch be captured and admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The sketch is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 572.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We turn, sir, to the issue of reports that were received by the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps. Could you remind the Trial Chamber which units of the 3rd Corps sent reports to the Intelligence Department?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command received reports from independent units, division commands, the 35th and the 37th Divisions. At the same time, reports were submitted by independent units, unless they were subordinated to a higher-ranking unit. Those units were the 303rd Mountain Brigade, the 330th Mountain Light Infantry Brigade, the 7th Muslim Brigade, and I mentioned the 314th Mountain Brigade yesterday. I apologise, if my apology can be taken into account. Why? Because the 314th Mountain Brigade, early 1995, and I can provide you with the exact date if that's necessary, was disbanded. Parts of that unit joined other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask, with the assistance of the Registrar, that the witness now be shown the document previously marked P02112. P02112.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interim intelligence report sent by the assistant commander for Intelligence of the 35th Division, submitted to the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command. This is marked "Priority," which means that it was supposed to be passed along as quickly as possible. If I look at the report and how it's made, I see that this gentleman is trying to inform us about the situation along the front line in his area of responsibility, in terms of intelligence; yet at the same time he's trying to inform us about the situation and activities being undertaken by the army's units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I draw your attention to paragraph 1 of this document, to the part of the document right above the little black dot, the first -- the top black dot on the left-hand side. Do you see a reference there, sir, to Odreda El-M?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this paragraph, what it says is this: "So far during combat operations, 30 Chetniks have been killed in the Potselovo sector. The their bodies remained on our side. Unofficial sources suggest that aggressor soldiers had been arrested as -- and one tank was seized from the El Mudjahedin Detachment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what would the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department do with the type of information contained in this report that you see before you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sort of information presented in this report is priority information, and this document contains information that had to be processed analytically as soon as possible. The officer in charge would inform himself about this situation, familiarise himself with the substance of any document that arrived, and he would immediately tell his direct superior, in this case this was the 3rd Corps commander, or anyone standing in for that person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I apologise for interrupting, but I think that there is some unclarity as to the interpretation of the passage that you drew the witness's attention to. In the translation, you can see it reads that: "Unofficial sources suggest aggressor soldiers were seized and one tank --" And I think the translation was "From the Mujahid Detachment," and that is not consistent with what is on the other screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, the sentence that contains the reference to Odreda "El-M," can you please read that sentence out again?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sentence reads as follows in Bosnian: "There is unofficial information that there are captured aggressor soldiers and a tank at the El Mudjahedin Detachment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And, Your Honours, we'll ask that this document be revised in terms of its translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But let me ask you this, sir: In the language of military intelligence, do you know what "unofficial sources" would refer to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When information is obtained, an assessment is made as to whether it is confirmed or unconfirmed. If the information is confirmed and if it is completely accurate, then this is immediately indicated, that this information is accurate and confirmed. If information is unconfirmed or if there is any doubt as to its credibility or accuracy, then an indication is made in the report whether this is confirmed or unconfirmed, official or unofficial. In the context of this document, this means that when Mr. Hajderhodzic indicated this was unofficial information, information from the unofficial sources, that means that this information was not confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we perhaps have the date of this document on the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, the heading of this document specifies the point in time where this -- when this document was made. Zavidovici, the 27th of May, 1995. Operational time, 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrkaljevic. The Prosecution would ask this document be admitted into evidence and we'll substitute a revised English translation once that's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 573.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would ask the witness now be shown Exhibit 554. Exhibit 554. And perhaps if we could scroll to the bottom of the B/C/S version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us who drafted this document?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am the author of this document, and this is a report where I inform or, rather, report to Mr. Husic. At the time when this document was drafted, Mr. Husic was at the forward command post of the 3rd Corps Command in the Orahovo sector. In order to facilitate orientation, Orahovo is northeast of Sarajevo, about 30 kilometres away. My responsibility was to send this report to Mr. Husic in order to inform him about the implementation of the task that had been received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask, and we could go to page -- the bottom of page 3 in the English version. Mr. Mrkaljevic, I would like to ask you about the paragraph that begins -- that you can see on the middle of the screen in front of you that begins: "O nasim aktivnostima ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, about the situation that you're describing in that paragraph, which in the English begins: "I briefed the commander ..." for reference of the Trial Chamber. Can you tell us about what you're reporting in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report, I describe the activities that were carried out in the course of that day. It reads as follows: "I briefed the commander of the 3rd Corps about our activities during the day, the briefing of the assistant commander for Intelligence and the current situation at a briefing held at 2200 hours. He agreed with the situation as it was presented and at the same time he approved the activities planned for today as follows: "Inspection of parts of the area of responsibility of the 328th Mountain Brigade in the grede Podsjelovo sector, focusing on analysing the situation at observation posts and their work; meet with the superior officer of the El Mudjahedin Detachment in order to seize part of the seized documents and request approval to contact the prisoners from the 1st Prnjavor Light Infantry Brigade who are located at their camp at the 14th kilometre towards Kamenica village."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some follow-up questions based on this part of your report, Mr. Mrkaljevic. In the first part of this paragraph, there's a reference to "the briefing of the assistant commander for Intelligence." Can you tell us, sir, to the best of your recollection, to whom you were referring when you wrote "the assistant commander for Intelligence"?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd, late at night, I set off from Orahovo to Sarajevo. I came to Zavidovici in the early morning hours. I rested a little bit, and between 12.30, at the forward command post of the 35th Division, I met the assistant commander for Intelligence, Mr. Izudin Hajderhodzic, where he briefed me, giving me an overview of the current situation in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division. I immediately made an arrangement with him. There is a restaurant, Panorama, Hotel Panorama, which is to the west of Zavidovici on the Krivaja River, and in two hours, in fact, the forward command post of the 3rd Corps was situated there, if necessary. So it was arranged that all the assistant commanders of all the units that were engaged in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division should go there in order to be briefed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about this meeting where you say, "I met the assistant commander for intelligence, Mr. Izudin Hajderhodzic, where he briefed me." What did he brief you about? What did he tell you about during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the meeting itself, he briefed me about the situation and some of the problems that had to do with an issue that he had already raised in his interim report. He told me that the information that the El Mudjahid Detachment, in its camp at the 14th kilometre, held about two or three, I don't know for sure, members of the 1st Prnjavor Light Brigade, was confirmed, so this information was confirmed. He gave me an overview of the situation on the front line, and he also informed me about the problems relating to the logistic support of observation posts. The main problem there was radio communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, again turning to the document, there's a reference to the fact that you briefed the commander of the 3rd Corps. When and where was that briefing?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefing of the 3rd Corps commander was held at the Panorama building. I indicated in this report that it was at 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt. On which day?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was all on the 24th, because when I came to Zavidovici I reported to the commander to let him know that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just for purposes of clarification, when you say "the 24th," can you tell us which month and year?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. The 24th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The transcript just indicated "May," sir. This document is dated after May. Can you clarify that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. My mistake. 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, when you said, as reflected on lines 1 and 2 of page 16: "I reported to the commander to let him know that I was there," which commander are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin, the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, Mr. Mrkaljevic, when you briefed Sakib Mahmuljin on 24 July 1995 at 2200 hours, what were the topics that you discussed with him in this briefing?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the usual procedure in intelligence affairs, when the commander is being briefed, a commander is told about the situation in the area of responsibility or that section of the area of responsibility where he is at the time with regard the enemy activities. Then the situation with regard to the current activities of persons and officers in the Intelligence Service, then the situation regarding the forthcoming activities of the persons in the Intelligence Service, and, if necessary, any other issues that might impinge on the execution of certain tasks, be it in terms of logistic support or any other aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, if we could go to the bottom of the Bosnian version of this page and to the bottom of page 3 in the English version, I'd like to ask you, sir, about that second bullet point that we were just discussing a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may just interrupt, Mr. Mundis, you asked the witness what were the topics that he discussed with Mr. Mahmuljin on the briefing of the 24th of July at 2200 hours. He has told us, in his answer, a general sketch of what is usually reported in accordance with the procedure. He hasn't told us the exact topics that were discussed that day. I would like to hear those topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I was attempting to do that by reference to the document, but I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you recall the specific topics that you briefed General Mahmuljin about at this briefing on 24 July 1995 at 2200 hours? What, specifically, did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, at the briefing for the commander of the 3rd Corps at 2200 hours, I informed him about the briefing that was received from the assistant commanders during the day, the assistant commanders for intelligence of the units engaged in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division. The second issue that I presented to the commander was the current intelligence situation, with some recently-acquired information about the enemy activities in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division. The third issue that I dealt with or, rather, that I reported on to the commander was the issue of the documents that had been seized, because from my contact with Mr. Edin Husic, it was suggested to me that I should not raise the issue of the captured members of the 1st Prnjavor Brigade because another service was dealing with that problem, which means that I did not brief the commander on the issue of the prisoners. The next issue on which I briefed the commander was the issue of the logistic support for the tasks whose implementation was planned in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, when you say, "I reported to the commander on the issue of the documents that had been seized," what documents are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During combat in the broader sector of Podsjelovo, members of the El Mujahid Detachment found some documents on the VRS troops that related to their units. The ID documents found on the persons were something that we needed to analyse them, and all the information, all the data that we could glean from them, were to be collated with the information or data that we already had at our disposal. This is standard operating procedure regarding any documents that are seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrkaljevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Were there -- did you find only ID documents -- I beg your pardon. Did the El Mudjahedin Detachment seize ID documents only or were there any other documents over and above the ID documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documents that were seized and that were taken over from the El Mudjahedin Detachment, when we're talking about this specific case, provided us with information that some ID documents had been obtained, and there were also several notebooks that were found with the members of the Republika Srpska Army, the first Prnjavor Brigade. But I have to say that we did not receive those documents immediately, as soon as we requested them. This was handed over to us in a period of time, maybe a month or a month and a half later, and it was handed over to Mr. Izudin Hajderhodzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, as reflected on page 18, lines 2 through 6, you told us: "Because from my contact with Mr. Edin Husic, it was suggested to me that I should not raise the issue of the captured members of the 1st Prnjavor Brigade because another service was dealing with that problem." Do you recall, sir, what other service was dealing with that problem?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem of the takeover of the captured Republika Srpska Army soldiers was in the purview of the Military Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask you if you could turn your attention back to the document on the screen in front of you and the second bullet point of the paragraph we were discussing before. Can you tell us, sir, what instructions you received from the 3rd Corps commander after you briefed him on 24 July 1995 at 2200 hours?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the commander received the report of the 24th of July, 1995, the 3rd Corps commander immediately approved that I may request the documents that had been seized. He gave his approval that there was a need to visit the area of responsibility of the 328th Mountain Brigade, to inspect it. That is the broader grede Podsjelovo sector. And combat operations reference that I referred to here were carried out in that area. And at the same time, when I made the request, he gave me the green light to use a car in order to carry out those activities. That was the car that had been used by operations officers to come to that area in the -- to that site in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, I'd like to focus your attention on the second bullet point, that is, not the part about Podsjelovo. Your document says "request approval to contact the prisoners of the 1st Prnjavor Light Infantry Brigade at their camp located 14 kilometres towards Kamenica village." And I'd like you to explain to us, sir, how that came to be written in your report.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this report. You can see up there in the heading, if we could scroll it up, please. This report was drafted at 1946 hours on the 24th of July, 1995, and as such, it was encrypted and sent to the forward command post at Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe you've told us earlier, sir, that this briefing that you had with the 3rd Corps commander was at 2200 hours on 24 July 1995. Can you explain how the document was --

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I did note that in the report, because I had already been in contact with the commander and he indicated that there would be this briefing at 2200 hours at the Panorama building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, can you explain to us, sir, how the document indicates that General Mahmuljin authorised you to take certain steps, if the document was sent before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you already, I had spoken to the commander of the record already by this time, and I told him about the situation. He agreed. I covered that information in my report. I informed Mr. Husic exactly what I had spoken to the commander about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us, sir, on page 18, lines 5 and 6: "I did not brief the commander on the issue of the prisoners." And in light of that testimony, I'd like to ask you to explain how your document indicates that General Mahmuljin requested you to contact the prisoners at the 14 km camp.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked him the question. Probably, and when I say "probably," probably he already had all the information on prisoners at his fingertips. In addition to that, this was to avoid any overlap between the various competences of people who were involved in the situation. That was another reason I didn't ask the question. And also I was trying to comply with the instructions I had received from Mr. Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, can you tell us what steps, if any, you took with respect to General Mahmuljin's order as reflected in the second bullet point of the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This second bullet, is that about the involvement so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could perhaps scroll down in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, this is a different portion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, sir, it's the same portion we've been discussing. It's the bullet point that says: "Meet with superior officer of the El Mudjahedin Detachment."

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an order by the corps commander. This is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, if we -- let me interrupt you there, because perhaps you can explain this, because the prefatory language of your report, which you've read out to us, indicates that you briefed the commander of the 3rd Corps. The second sentence says: "He agreed with the presented situation and approved the following activities planned for today." Is that what your report says, sir?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. A specific situation was issued. He agreed to this. He gave the green light, and he gave the go-ahead to the activities for the 27th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrkaljevic, when you say, "He agreed to this, he gave the green light, he gave the go-ahead," to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I'm referring to me, that I should carry out these activities that I had previously put forward to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, but I'm asking you who the "he" was. You told us, "He agreed to this, he gave the green light, he gave the go-ahead." Who is the "he" that you're referring to and that's referred to in your document?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. The reference was to the 3rd Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, based on your testimony and what the document says, it indicates that he approved the following activities, and the "he" being General Mahmuljin, he agreed and approved for you to meet the superior officer of the El Mudjahedin Detachment. That's what the second bullet point of your document says. What steps, if any, did you take --

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps, sir, if any, did you take to comply with what was written in second bullet point of your document, Exhibit 554?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th of July, 1995, in the morning hours, in a motor vehicle, accompanied by Mr. Izudin Hajderhodzic from Zavidovici, we arrived in the general Livade village area. This is an area south of grede Podsjelovo. At the time, the Command of the El Mudjahedin Detachment was located there. On our arrival in Livade village, we found a place where there were several houses, and that's where the El Mudjahid Detachment Command was. At a distance of 150 to 200 metres from there, we were pulled over by two armed members of the El Mudjahid Detachment. They didn't allow us to pass. We had to wait there. A person came up of Afro-Asian origin. That was my take, at least. I think the name was Ajman Awar [as interpreted] or something like that. I'm not exactly certain. We talked to this person. We talked about the hand-over of the documents that had been seized. Several minutes later, after 10.00, he promised that he would see the commander of the El Mujahid Detachment about this and that they would see what could be done about this. I pressed him on it, saying that he should do this immediately, talk to the commander of the El Mudjahid Detachment, I mean, so that I might know whether the seized documents would be handed over to us immediately by the El Mujahid Detachment or not. He categorically refused, saying, "When the time comes, this will be dealt with." He turned away from us and walked away towards the buildings where the El Mujahid Detachment Command used to be. I had no choice but to turn to my colleague, Mr. Izudin, get back in our vehicle, and drive back to Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just get clarification here? You said, "On our arrival in Livade village." Do I understand you to say that Livade village is the same place as the camp which is located 14 kilometres towards Kamenica village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, then I would like you to clarify. The document says that Mr. Mahmuljin approved that you meet with the superior officer of the El Mudjahedin Detachment to remove part of the seized documents and request approval to contact the prisoners of the 1st Infantry -- okay, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also note the time, and I am aware of the fact that I've gone over the amount of time I'd estimated for the direct. I would again ask if I could have a little bit of additional time following the break to just wrap up a couple of issues, and then I'll cease with the direct examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well. Are you saying this is a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mrkaljevic, earlier this morning, in response to a question, I believe, from the Bench, you talked about the documents that are referred to in Exhibit 554, which is the document that's in front of you. Can you tell us, sir, to the best of your recollection, when you received the documents referred to in this paragraph of your document?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents referred to in this paragraph are documents that were seized throughout this period by the 1st Prnjavor Brigade. We didn't personally receive those. The documents never reached the Intelligence Department. They were included in an intelligence report, and Mr. Izudin Hajderhodzic processed these documents for the purpose of that report, and there was a delay, as I pointed out already, a delay of about a month or a month and a half. I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The document in front of you, sir, also, as we've discussed earlier, makes reference to the "logor" or camp at 14 km near Kamenica. You told us a few moments ago that you and Mr. Hajderhodzic went to Livade. Did you, sir, at any point in time, in accordance with the approval you received from General Mahmuljin, did you at any point in time go to the 14 km camp in order to see the prisoners referred to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While on that point, I just want to ask the question: When you talked to the gentleman you say you think his name is Ajman, after you had been pulled off 150 to 200 metres from their camp, did you raise the question of the prisoners with him, because you've only told us about the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was talking about the documents that were seized, and I didn't raise the issue of POWs at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've stated the reason already. My superior, Edin Husic, made the suggestion that I should not raise the issue of the POWs of the 1st Prnjavor Light Infantry Brigade at all, just to make sure there was no overlap between the various competences. This was an issue dealt with by the Military Security Service, because that was within their purview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understood you to say that you didn't raise that issue when you talked to Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin. But this document here says Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin has approved that you go and talk to the superior officer of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, to remove the documents and to request approval to see the prisoners. So -- let me finish. So I would expect that when you went to Livade, you were going to deal with two issues, the question of documents and the question of prisoners. You had approval to deal with the question of prisoners, according to this document. Are you now saying, notwithstanding this approval to find out about prisoners, you still decided not to deal with the question of prisoners when you got to Livade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said before, at the briefing, when I informed the commander about this, I never raised anything to do with POWs, because my own superior, Edin Husic, had previously made the suggestion to me that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that part, sir. Please, let's get on a little bit, let's make progress. I hear you on that point. I'm talking now about Exhibit 554 that is before you. Exhibit 554 before you, notwithstanding you having not raised the issue of prisoners of war with Mr. Mahmuljin, Mr. Mahmuljin is giving you approval here to raise the issue with the El Mudjahedin Detachment, and I'm asking you: Did you raise the issue with the El Mudjahedin Detachment when you met this man in Livade? And if you didn't, why didn't you? Because you've got the approval, unless I'm misunderstanding something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I met the members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, I didn't raise the issue of POWs. I didn't raise the issue because I had previously received instructions from my superior, Mr. Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know whether the security people within the 3rd Corps did follow up the question of prisoners of war, now that you didn't deal with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't, but if I bear in mind the instructions that I received from my superior, Edin Husic, the suggestion that he made, I think it likely that because it would have been one of their responsibilities, that service would have been on the job already by this time. When I say "likely," I mean this: I was never in touch with anyone from that service at the time. I never talked to any of them about this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you and Mr. Hajderhodzic went to Livade just to talk about those documents; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know if Mr. Hajderhodzic had ever been to Livade previously to deal with POWs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had been to Livade, yes, but I can't say for sure whether he asked any members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment to see the prisoners. He never told me anything about that himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, on at least one occasion this morning, and perhaps two, you've mentioned this person, Iaman, that you encountered in Livade when you went there with Mr. Hajderhodzic. Other than that instance in Livade, sir, did you on any other occasion have any interaction with this person, Iaman?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not hold any meetings with that person over the ensuing period of time or at all, for that matter. That was the first time I met him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Had you ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry to do this to you. This name, "Iaman," is being spelled quite a number of times, and Madam Vidovic warned us about this the other day. I thought "Ajman" is spelled A-J-M-A-N, not "Iaman," or is it a different name, this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I don't want to be in a position of testifying, but I believe sometimes in the documents the name is transliterated in different ways, and there are different spellings in documents, and perhaps with different court reporters, occasionally we get different spellings as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I just hope when we read this three months' down the line, we'll be able to see it for "Eimen."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours, and I also know that when it comes to searching, electronically searching transcripts that this raises a whole host of issues which I have raised on a number of occasions with both the interpretation booth and the court reporters and discussed with my learned colleagues from the Defence as well. It is a slight problem, and again it's also reflected in documents where names are transliterated in various ways, particularly names that might have originally been in a language other than B/C/S or English, and I'll simply leave that, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you just told us, as reflected on lines 4 and 5 of page 29: "This was the first time I met him in person." Had you ever seen this person, Ajman, before, or heard his name before?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen Ajman before. I had heard his name from colleagues who were, in a way, in touch with him occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "colleagues," sir, to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some colleagues from the Military Security Service who pointed out sometimes off the record that they had met Ajman. Was this the same person, was this not the same person? I can hardly say. I did not, myself, attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, you also told me, or answered in response to a question I asked you a few moments ago, about the 14 km camp, that you did not, on the 25th of July, 1995, go to that location. For purposes of clarification, sir, were you at any point in time in the camp at 14 km, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. In some reports, this is referred to as a camp. Technically speaking, the true definition of that location would be a deployment sector, because that is or was where a unit was stationed. This is near the Gostovici River. The 14-kilometre reference is the distance between the location and the town of Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, that a unit was stationed there, what unit are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the El Mudjahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there any other what you've called deployment sectors of the El Mudjahedin Detachment along the Gostovici River?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in part also in Borovica village along the Gostovic River. They were staying in a number of family homes there, and also at the 14-kilometre location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 511.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the operations log or operations diary that is kept at the command post of a unit. In this particular case, this is the operations diary kept by the duty officer at the forward command post of the 3rd Corps. In the broader sector of the Kamenica village, the site is Luke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please go, in the Bosnian version of this document, to the page bearing ERN number 0185-5080. And in the English version, we need to go to the same, the page bearing the same ERN number. If we could scroll up to the top in the Bosnian, please, or top half of the document. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you opening the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now we seem to have lost the Bosnian version. And if we could go to the top half of the Bosnian version and the top of the page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, I would draw your attention to the handwritten material that is between entry number 308 and entry number 309 and ask you if you can tell us what is reflected by the information that's written there.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, in the part that you referred to, it is indicated that duty was handed over by Jusuf Halilagic, and that I personally, Sejfulah Mrkaljevic, took over as the duty officer. And you can see our signatures here. It's an issue that I assumed as the duty officer at the Luke forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, on what date did you assume command at the Luke forward -- or assume the role of duty officer at the Luke forward command post on this date, as reflected in these entries?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hand-over of duty at the forward command post was usually done in the morning, between 7.30 and 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And my question, sir, is: This part of the logbook that we're looking at, or the diary, what date or dates does this indicate that you took over as duty officer from Mr. Halilagic?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under entry 309, this is the chronological order of the receipt of information. The time indicated here is 1400 hours, and the date is the 13th of September, and this is 1995. And the text reads as follows: "Urgent call for the commander from General Delic. He is to call him at the IKM of the General Staff in Visoko."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, just a couple of clarifying questions, if I may. When you say "urgent call for the commander," what commander are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference is Commander Sakib Mahmuljin, the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, "he is to call him," what are you -- what are you writing down or what is being noted in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entry here, I don't know if you have an original page where an entry is made, where you can see the headings, and you have the column 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, and the header -- the table header, if I may explain this briefly, specify first the number under which the information was recorded. If you allow me, I know that this is a little bit extensive, but I have to elaborate. And then in column 2, it is stated that the time when the information was received or a document was received, and the date. Column 3, the kind of information, whether it was in the textual form or perhaps a document. Thank you very much, precisely. And then column 4, from whom to whom it is being forwarded. And column 5 is the signature of the officer or person who received information or a document. I think that now I managed to provide clarification for a number of issues that may arise from this entry, could we now please go back to the actual entry? And here, in column 4, this is all in my handwriting. It is indicated as follows -- could you please zoom in on column 4. Excellent, thank you. Could you scroll down a little bit there just below my signature. "Gentlemen, it is stipulated quite specifically OKM 3 KOC IKM," and my initials are there. And this means that I received the information from the office of the commander of the 3rd Corps. I cannot now tell you specifically whether it was relayed to me by the commander's secretary or one of the officers who usually were there in the office, and I immediately forwarded this information to the Operations Centre of the forward command post of the 3rd Corps, because the commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin, was not present at Luke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mrkaljevic, can you explain to us -- you just said, "I cannot now tell you specifically whether it was relayed to me by the commander's secretary or one of the officers who usually were there in the office." What are you referring to when you told us that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I explained that to you, I meant that I personally did not take that phone call from General Delic. This means that the telephone call had not come from General Delic, but this was just a piece of information that was relayed, that the commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin, should urgently report to or call General Delic at the forward command post of the General Staff in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're all clear, sir, when you say, "This means that the telephone call had not come from General Delic," from whom did the call come? Who called you, in other words?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given information from the OKM of the 3rd Corps in Zenica. I cannot now tell you whether I received this information from the lady who was Sakib Mahmuljin's secretary at the basic command post in Zenica or whether this was relayed to me by an officer who was in Commander Sakib Mahmuljin's office at the basic command post of the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "OKM," what does that abbreviation refer to?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The abbreviation OKM refers to basic command post of the 3rd Corps, and it was located in Zenica, as I have already explained to you. It was in Technoprojekt building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What's the difference between a basic command post of the 3rd Corps and the 3rd Corps headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no difference. The command building, that's what it is. In military parlance, we refer to it as a basic command post. So when I was telling you where the headquarters of the 3rd Corps were, I in fact meant the basic command post. That's one and the same thing. Or, rather, to make it easier for you, that's the main command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Mrkaljevic, do you recall where General Mahmuljin was on 14 September 1995 at approximately 1400 hours, when you received this phone call as reflected on line 309 of Exhibit 511?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to avoid any confusion, the date in the diary is the 13th, not the 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where General Mahmuljin was on 13 September 1995, at approximately 1400 hours when you received this phone call that's reflected on line 309 of Exhibit 511?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I received the phone call, I can't tell you where the commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin, was. But I do know that he was in the field. When I say "in the field," I assume that he was with one of the units or that he was in a meeting with somebody somewhere, because I checked, and at that time he was not at the forward command post in Luke. And I immediately relayed this information to the Operations Centre, and the Operations Centre is the centre where all the communication equipment is, and they are responsible for informing the commander -- they were responsible to inform the commander about this phone call, using communications equipment. When I say "commander," I mean Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrkaljevic. The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before Madam Vidovic takes over the cross-examination, I would like to get some little clarification on Exhibit 554. Could we have it, please. Could we go to that page where we were talking about the approval to do certain things. Right. Sir, can you just explain to us what these abbreviations mean, you know, in this paragraph. "I briefed the commander of the 3rd Corps about our activities during the day, the briefing of PK for ObP." What do those --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "PK for ObP" is an abbreviation for assistant commander for Intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mrkaljevic.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you some questions on behalf of General Rasim Delic, as his Defence counsel. The nature of the cross-examination is such that you will be able to answer many of my questions with a simple "yes" or "no," but if you feel that you need to provide any further explanations, please do so. Since we speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to make a pause between my question and your answer in order for the record to be able to keep up with us. First of all, Mr. Mrkaljevic, I would like to ask you, what kind of education have you had in your civilian life?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My education in the civilian life is as follows: In 1977, I completed three years of secondary education. It was a school for mechanical engineering. In 1984 and 1985, I completed the fourth and the fifth educational degrees, again in mechanical engineering. And then in early 1986, I reported to the Republican Department for the Exploitation of Coal Mines in Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to take the Republican examination for the independent operator in underground exploitation of coal in coal mines in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I managed to complete that within the stipulated time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, the education that you received before the war, as a civilian, enabled you to work in technical jobs in a coal mine; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. In order to clarify things a bit, I was working on the maintenance of the underground coal mine exploitation in a coal mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, where did you complete this -- the fourth and the fifth degree of your education?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fourth and the fifth degree of my education were completed in Zenica. That was a department of the Workers University, and this was -- the courses were held in the secondary school for mechanical engineering in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you did your national service in the Reserve Officers School in Zadar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This school trains the cadets for the tasks of platoon commanders; is that so, in essence?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in essence, that is so in infantry. But as I indicated earlier, I completed the Reserve Officers School for anti-aircraft artillery and rocket units in the former JNA, which means, in military parlance, that I was trained to command a battery of anti-aircraft weapons. And just to make a comparison, with the infantry that would be the company-level command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm driving at, what I'm interested in, is you were trained to operate anti-aircraft weapons in the army?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in the course of my training and my internship after I completed this level of education, as an officer in the former JNA I held the rank of a sergeant. We carried out tasks that were closely linked with the infantry too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mrkaljevic, I have a number of questions, so I would kindly like to ask you to answer my questions as briefly as you can, in particular in this segment of my cross-examination. What I want to know is the following: You did not undergo any kind of training for intelligence work before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, in 1986, during the two-month training in the training centre in Derventa, that's the training centre of the former Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, I received training for the infantry company commander, and at the same time, as part of that training, we went through some topics that had to do with intelligence work. And I'm sorry I'm taking your time, but this had to do with how to establish observation posts in infantry, how they should operate, what the observers should do, what their duties were and responsibilities, and how they were to go about carrying it out. So -- and there was also some abridged training for the gathering and processing of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but apart from what you've just told us, the two-month course that you just described to us, you did not undergo any intelligence officer training. What you just described to us is not intelligence officer training?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, because the former Yugoslav People's Army had special centres where intelligence officers were trained, and I did not undergo that kind of training.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was in Pancevo, and you did not undergo that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was known colloquially as "the 5.000 training."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not undergo any training for a security officer?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not graduate from a military academy?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a graduate of the military academy. I wanted to do so, but it was not possible. But in the Reserve Officers School in the former JNA, it is some kind of a abridged form of a military academy training.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this abridged form of a military academy training, it takes six months instead of four years; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you call it, the abridged military academy training, you did not receive any training for a military officer work?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was not supposed to train for the intelligence officer. My branch was anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you left the JNA with the rank of a second lieutenant, and when the war started, you had the rank of a lieutenant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the JNA with the rank of a sergeant, and pursuant to a degree, I was promoted to the rank of the second lieutenant. That was an automatic promotion. And later on, I was promoted to lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that on the average, the former JNA -- the practice in the former JNA was that a reserve officer would be promoted to a new rank every four years; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but provided that in that period, that officer had participated in a certain number of exercises with his unit, and that was the basic precondition for the promotion to the next higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I conclude that in this period of 12 years, you did not take part in the exercises, that you did not participate in a sufficient number of exercises to be promoted, because you were promoted only by one rank in the 12-year period?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I did not participate in anti-aircraft defence exercises because the exercises for those units were not held all that often, because they were quite expensive in terms of equipment and they were quite complicated, and also I did not volunteer to participate in exercises, but you had to be assigned by somebody.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please understand, I'm not trying to criticise you. I'm just trying to ascertain what the facts are. How many drills did you have over that time?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I understand your question, and my answer reflects that. The drills that I did, I did whenever I was summoned by my superiors to go there and attend one of those drills.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There weren't that many, after all. How many would you say?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my recollection, three or four. A few, very few. Certainly not enough to get a promotion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this all had to do with anti-aircraft defence; it didn't have anything to do with intelligence business, did it?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In 1986, after I had completed my training in Derventa, I became the commander of a TO detachment in charge of the mines at Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's start with the relevant questions. While testifying yesterday, you said that in May 1993, you started your service with the 3rd Corps of the BH Army; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in early May, the first half of May 1993, I was transferred from the 303rd to the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you became an intelligence desk officer; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to be able to do that job properly, one would have needed a certain amount of knowledge in order to be able to understand any information being received, in order to have a military familiarity with this kind of information and in order to be able to process such information; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 50/50, I would say. You are right to some degree, but not entirely, because whoever knows anything about anything, whoever is familiar with the goings on of our day-to-day existence know something about how intelligence is gathered. Therefore, I can say that when I first came to work there, this was something entirely new to me, but I only took a very brief time to master the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that one of your principal tasks was to draft technical assessments and prepare proposals?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this required some sort of technical military knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be the case, but each of my assessments applied, and I think my work had a lot of validity; at least to me it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree -- let me ask you this: Do you agree that the corps commander is a very high-ranking command?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being familiar with the military terminology, the Corps Command is a command where only those officers could work that held the highest ranks. The level back in the JNA would have been major, colonel, lieutenant colonel, major general, lieutenant general, and up from there, officers with a very strong military background and training, officers who were very experienced and who had long stints in the army behind them already.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. This is the way I see it: You came to work there. Your job required a certain military rank, major, for example, military background, military knowledge, military academy, and so on and so forth. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are entirely right. But if you turn back a couple of pages in that particular book, you will realise that in the regular Army of the BH, there were certain ranks you will see, who did what, and if you look at the overall situation that prevailed at the time, this should become clear to you. I was no exception, if you look at the officers who were in such jobs at the time. There was no straying from the standard at all, if you look at what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm trying to ask you. You and your colleagues from the 3rd Corps did not have the requisite training to perform their jobs at such a high-ranking command as the 3rd Corps Command; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the BH Army, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "the BH Army," I mean the BH Army in its entirety. It was created from nothing, literally from scratch.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I see what you mean. You came in May 1993, you joined the corps. You must know, then, that the corps wasn't established -- or rather its establishment had not been ordered before the end of 1992 and early 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, madam. I'm quite familiar with the procedure regarding the establishment of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going into that. I will just be asking you to tell me about a number of peculiarities that had to do with this. Would you agree that even in peace time, a corps like that would take a long time to set up? You came there and you saw what the situation was and what it meant; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the situation, and I know full well that in order to set up a unit or a command of corps level, in my assessment this might take between one year and one and a half years, roughly speaking. There needs to be a filtering process in terms of the officers joining the corps. One must train them, and then there should be a test of their abilities and aptitude for carrying out certain assignments and tasks in those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you this, too: The personnel-related problems that you talked about, the fact that many men were not properly trained, do you agree that the situation was even more difficult across the brigades than in the corps?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's self-implicit, isn't it? If I may just explain this, in my work, especially at the level of the 3rd Corps, we were facing a great deal of hardship and problems, because over a very short period of time, especially at the initial stage, there was a huge influx of officers that simply passed through our service; not just officers, ordinary soldiers, too. We had to do daily repetitions of certain things. We had to take to the field, speak to local commanders to stop this situation, to bring things -- to take things back where they used to be in order to achieve a quality level that would have allowed us to perform certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you have enumerated for us some units from which the 3rd Corps Command was receiving reports. You mentioned the 35th Division, the 37th Division, the 303rd Brigade, the 330th Brigade, the 7th Muslim Brigade. And just to clarify matters here, these were units that were directly subordinated to the 3rd Corps; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. And as I've mentioned before, it was a slip of the tongue on my part in relation to this period, because what I'm talking about is the 314th Brigade midway through 1995, because as far as I know, in early 1995 it was disbanded and then parts of this unit were redeployed and joined other units, the 303rd, the 330th and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
