utterances.text: All right. Let's just clarify matters a little bit. When you talked about receiving reports, what you have in mind from these units you just enumerated, what you have in mind is the period of 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, the period that I was actually asked about by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So these brigades that you mentioned, these were independent brigades under the 3rd Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were independent brigades under the 3rd Corps, unless in some aspects or at certain times they were resubordinated to another high-ranking unit. In this specific situation, it could have been the 35th Division or the 37th Division, within the structure and the makeup of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right. All right. The 7th Muslim Brigade, during the events that you witnessed in 1995, it wasn't resubordinated to the 35th Division, was it? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific period in time, you mean? Units of the 35th Division were active in the area. The El Mudjahid Detachment, the 375th Light Brigade, the joint detachment of the joint battalion of the 303, 330 and 319, and an incomplete battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade. So it wasn't an entire brigade that was resubordinated to the 35th Division, it was these units that I have just listed for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's all I wanted to clarify. Thank you. Whatever the case may be, the 3rd Corps never received reports from the brigades that were part of the 35th or 37th Divisions; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. If we had been receiving reports from them, that would have been a direct violation of the subordination system.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you about -- let me ask you about something that you said yesterday and today. You spoke about the reporting system down the intelligence line; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say that units were supposed to submit intelligence reports; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I said "were supposed to submit those," I said nothing about the circumstances surrounding this process. And, secondly, the circumstances at times made it impossible for them to submit reports in a timely manner. Our officers made every effort to deal with their tasks and assignments in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember that the reports you were receiving, I'm talking about the quality of those reports, the quality hinged directly on the quality of incoming intelligence and the accuracy of incoming intelligence, I mean intelligence being received from people who were out in the field?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, your assessment is entirely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Say, for example, you weren't on the ground, you weren't in an area where a certain thing was happening. It would have been very difficult for you to take in what the situation really was, would it not?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So suppose you went somewhere in the field. Suppose you had no report. You would never know whether your information, the information that you were receiving, was complete and accurate, would you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to put this as mildly as possible. We tried to speak to each and every officer we had. We tried to get them to study, cross-reference and double-check any information received before it was submitted to the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll be returning to that issue at a later stage, but now I will ask you something about your evidence yesterday. You said that you were receiving information from people in the field. You would process this information, and then -- and then this information would be submitted to the Intelligence Administration in Sarajevo or, alternatively, in Kakanj. All right, this is what I'll ask you questions about. First of all, you knew that there was a command post of the General Staff in Kakanj throughout 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about a command post, sir.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you must add this little word, "forward," because that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it is your belief that this was, in fact, a forward command post; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, that is my belief. If I may -- if I may explain, and if you could compare that to the explanation that I provided to the OTP when they asked me about the basic command post and the forward command post --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No need, Mr. Mrkaljevic. Can you just please stick to answering my questions, kindly. Whatever we call it, "command post" or "forward command post," what I mean to ask you is the following: You were an intelligence officer. You knew that this command post was monitoring combat operations and the planning of combat operations in certain cases; you did know that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, madam. However, we produced reports for the Intelligence Administration at times because of orders received from our superiors, the late General Mustafa Hajrulahovic, for example, were forwarded also to the command post in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: One step at a time, please. Do you agree that certain officers from the Intelligence Administration were responsible for the planning and monitoring of combat operations, and some of those were, in fact, based in Kakanj throughout 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that intelligence reports from people, officers working in the field, were essential to them precisely because they were monitoring combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is self-evident, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And yet you can't tell us exactly what sort of information was being sent to Kakanj and what other sort of information was being sent to Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary, in fact. I can say exactly. I did the same report, the same assessments, the same weekly summary reports, the same information letters, the same conclusions. The header would normally read "Intelligence Administration of the General Staff of the BH Army," paragraph 1, paragraph 2. And of course as I said before, if the late General Hajrulahovic so ordered, in the second paragraph there would be this: "Intelligence Department, Kakanj Forward Command Post."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree with me that accurate information about who you sent these reports to and who actually received it could be seen if we actually had those documents available to us, the documents you're talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, madam. If you go to the archive, you will see all the documents, who they were addressed to and who they were forwarded to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that the most reliable information as to the fact whether a document was sent or received by anyone is what is written on the document itself?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned General Hajrulahovic, and I noted that you said "late General Hajrulahovic." Could you please help us? He was your superior officer. When did General Mustafa Hajrulahovic die, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was -- another question to ask, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you know. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say it was in early 1998. I'm really embarrassed. I don't know the exact date, but I think that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me go back to the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps. You explained to us in detail the structure of the intelligence organ in the 3rd Corps. You described the sections, the analysis section, the planning section, the section for cooperation with international organisations, and the section that dealt with electronic reconnaissance. You told us that that section -- that section had 13 employees?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Intelligence Department had between 12 and 14 staff. At some points in time, it was 12. At other points, it was 14. Let me just give you an example. Over a period of maybe two months, I would say two, three or four staff under me in my section saw there was a great deal of people coming in and out of the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you: Of the 13 staff in the Intelligence Department, could you please tell the Trial Chamber how many of them were graduates of a military academy?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the 3rd Corps Intelligence Department only Mr. Edin Husic was a graduate of a military academy, Mr. Samir Sakic was a graduate, Mr. Emin Prijic was a graduate of a secondary military school. I had completed the Reserve Officers School, and there were some other officers who had completed military secondary schools. And the other officers mostly had civilian jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The way I understand you, two of them were graduates of the military academy. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that Mr. Husic did not have intelligence expertise, he did not receive that kind of military training specific for intelligence officers?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, just before the war he graduated from the military academy, so I can only assume -- I cannot tell you that with any certainty, but I assume that he did not have a sufficient degree of knowledge or expertise in the intelligence work. The other gentleman that was a graduate of the military academy, Samir Sakic, he completed it just before the war also, and he was -- his specialty was armoured units. This was an additional problem in our work, but I would like you to go back to what I said about the army as a whole. This was an inevitable consequence of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But what I am trying to find out here is to clarify the level of expertise among the people who worked in intelligence. My next question is the following: You described to us how you did your analysis. Before joining the analysis section, could you please tell the Trial Chamber how many kinds of analysis had you drafted up until that time in your entire life?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until my arrival in the 3rd Corps Command, I had drafted a couple of analyses in the operations organ of the 303rd Mountain Brigade, and I remember that I did a couple of analyses as a reserve lieutenant, but the analyses primarily had to do with the readiness for the performance of certain tasks. In other words, they were not directly linked with intelligence work. I can see here that I have to tell you, when I said that in 1986 I took the exam for the underground coal exploitation before a Republican inspector, I received approval from the highest level of the Republican authorities to be able to work independently on the underground exploitation of coal, and let me tell you, performing this kind of job is commensurately -- involves a higher responsibility than any job in the army that I had, so I know and you know that when I worked in a coal pit that was the second most dangerous coal pit in the world, I know that it might not seem that way to you, you might not accept that, but Raspotocje coal pit was the second most dangerous coal pit, the concentration of methane and so on. That's where I worked, and I had 35 people working for me, and I was responsible for them. And while I worked there, nobody was killed or injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, I understand that, I understand the importance of your work, but I'm trying to get to the facts that are relevant for us, and I want to find out what you know about that. I'm not here to challenge your abilities. Please don't take it that way. Let me go back to what we were talking about, but, Your Honours, I see that it is time now for our break. I can then continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We'll take the break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, you told us about the sources that your department, the department where you worked, used to get the intelligence. I asked you a little while ago about how you received information from the subordinate units, so I will not be asking you about that. I will be going back to that a bit later with regard to specific documents. But I want to ask you something else in this regard. Yesterday, you told us about other sources that were available, and you mentioned the documents that were seized from the enemy; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you said professional literature. What kind of literature did you mean, the kind that you seized from the enemy or literature that the BH Army had? What do you mean by that? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about professional literature, I meant the literature concerning the enemy forces, their professional literature that came into our possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Do you agree with me that you didn't have much of that kind of literature, you did not come by it all that often?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions in which we worked were below minimum, because we had to start from scratch. Right at the beginning, we encountered many difficulties. We didn't have this kind of professional literature at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also didn't have other equipment such as, for instance, night-vision equipment and other kinds of equipment that intelligence officers need in order to be able to get a full picture?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The equipment that the units -- intelligence units and intelligence officers should have in order to be able to monitor the situation adequately. You also mentioned the night-vision equipment and other types of equipment used to monitor the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, you told us that media were a source, the media from the other side in the conflict, that this was yet another source of information that you used, and now I want to ask you something in this regard. You will agree with me that in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the media played a very important role in fomenting inter-ethnic hatred?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right on that account. They were the key factor, both the audio and visual media, they were one of the key factors in the breakup of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there was a high degree of hatred and mistrust in the Croatian and Serbian media aimed at the people who were loyal to the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree fully with you. What you say is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at a document. Could the witness please look at Exhibit 235. Do you agree -- okay, let's wait for the English version. But can I ask you to look at the first part of this document while we're waiting for the English version. Do you agree that you have in front of you a press release from the 3rd Corps Press Centre? The date is the 11th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You worked there at the time. I want to ask you now to read the first two passages to yourself.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that lies are being disseminated through the media in the neighbouring state of Croatia, and it says further on that the purpose is to deepen the rift between the Croatian and Muslim peoples. Would you agree with this statement, that very often lies were disseminated through the media in Croatia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am very familiar with that. The people in Croatia and Serbia were served the kind of information that the politicians wanted them to have for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of this is the following: You told us that the media were used as a source of intelligence, either TV broadcasts or the press. How could you then -- this is a report from the very same corps where you served. How could you then take seriously what is written in the media and put it in your analysis if we are talking about this kind of reporting in Croatian and Serbian media?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me explain this to you and to the Trial Chamber. If, for instance, you have the Herzeg-Bosna radio station in Kakanj, and if they have some kind of a show and then they mention somebody, a name and they say, "Dear Marko, your family wishes to say hello to you," or, "Sorry you are not here with us," you -- and say that he is stationed at such-and-such a place at such-and-such a unit, we take this information, we process it, and then we collate it, we classify it, and it is useful to us. We learn from this kind of information about the deployment of certain HVO units, where units are deployed, on what section of the front line facing us. So when I said that we were monitoring the public media, the press, radio or TV, when I said that those were our sources of information, this is the way in which we obtain intelligence that was useful for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But let me just clarify this. If the media, for instance, report that the Muslim forces killed a hundred or 200 people, captured so many people, how did you treat this information? Was that relevant to you? What did you do with that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we knew that this was, in fact, disinformation, not information, in the true sense of the word, because disseminating this kind of information served the purpose of creating the impression under one's own populace that the Muslim forces had perpetrated a massacre, killed so many people and so on and so forth. We did not take that into account at all because we knew that it was disinformation. When I explained to the Prosecutor yesterday the role played by one of the subsections in the Intelligence Department that dealt with this, there were two and sometimes three officers in the Intelligence Department who monitored these reports, reports of this kind in the media. They also read the press from the other side. They studied those reports, and they immediately submitted reports where they classified those bits and pieces as either information or misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But at any rate, you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not monitor the media. I didn't do this kind of task.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me ask you something else. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 570. Witness, do you remember that you saw this document yesterday? It was about your appointment. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my promotion, yes, and I commented on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Could we now please go to page 2 of this document, the signature specifically. That is also the last page in both versions, the English and the B/C/S. The English. Right. Your Honours, could we please zoom in on the stamp. All right. There is a part of the -- yeah, right, this is fine. This is fine, thank you. Leave it like that. Witness, you saw that this was a document of the Supreme Command Staff. Do you agree with me that the stamp belongs to the Supreme Command Staff? You can clearly see that it says "Supreme Command Staff, Army General Delic." Can you see another word right there, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not General Delic's signature. That's the first thing. This is his stamp, stamp number 3, but that's different. Normally, number 3 stamps were used by personnel officers in staffs and commands, and the little word there is "for" or "on behalf of." I don't know who initialled or signed this document. I can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record and also for the OTP's benefit, I think the document should be re-translated, because the English version, as far as I see, has no indication that this is signed on behalf of or for someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Mundis, do you have anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We can either submit the document for revision or simply take the transcript, as it's indicated clearly on the Bosnian version, we can see the handwriting "za" which there's no dispute that means "for" or "signed on behalf of." There's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can put this away now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday and today, you were asked questions about the Mujahedin. As far as I understand your evidence, you have precious little personal knowledge about the Mujahedin, do you not?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I wouldn't agree with your statement. It's not about knowledge. I've explained this already. I had very little experience that I acquired through direct experience with them, through meeting them, which means I didn't have the sort of experience that would have told me how to treat these people and how to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You remember saying to the investigators of the OTP -- or rather making a statement to them on the 28th of February?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe it would be a good idea to show the witness D549. This is a tape, 7248, page B7 out of 18, and page 112 of the Bosnian transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, you see the Bosnian version as we are waiting for the English to come up. I will quote this portion of the transcript for you. You said: "When it comes to the El Mudjahedin Detachment," that we mentioned yesterday, "I previously mentioned the problems and difficulties that we had in communication with that unit. I personally never had an opportunity to get in touch with any members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment, and I never received any indication from my superior officer that he had ever had an opportunity to contact members of the El Mudjahedin Detachment." Let me ask you, first of all, this truly reflects your words, the words you shared with the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "superior officer," you mean Mr. Edin Husic; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's who I mean. He was my direct superior at the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Further, in answer to this question by the OTP, you said: "Yes, Edin Husic, that's who I'm referring to, so for this reason I cannot recall that any information at all ever came from the El Mudjahedin Detachment about the enemy or its deployment from the El Mudjahedin Detachment to the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps"?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we just scroll the document down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you said to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said to the investigators, and I stand by that. As chief of the analysis sector, I never received a single letter in writing from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If we could please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There seems to be some sort of an unclarity in the English translation. At page -- at line number 20, where the witness confirms that he's speaking about Edin Husic, he continues to say that, "So for the above reasons, I cannot recall that any piece of information ever came from the El Mujahid about the enemy," and then he goes on to say, "or its deployment from El Mujahid to the intelligence department of the 3rd Corps." What exactly is that supposed to mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it should mean that the translation is not accurate. I just quoted what's written there. "I can't remember that any information on the enemy forces ever reached the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, can the speakers please be asked not to overlap and speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are asked not to speak at the same time, please. Don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, about this, I showed you this section because I was asked to ask you something else. Based on this, I conclude that you never had an opportunity to contact anyone from the El Mudjahedin Detachment. Right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I stated in my evidence that on the 24th of July, 1995, I contacted -- well, I can tell you exactly who it was, Ajman. I see that there was some confusion about that. That was the first time I met that person. It could have been someone else altogether. I simply didn't know him, but that's what he said his name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you about the detachment specifically, so I wish to say something else about that. You never received any intelligence from them, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You never received any information on their victims?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Their plans?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their plans, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You didn't know what the composition of those units was, who there was in that detachment; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, then: You said a while ago they had another HQ in Borovica. Actually, what you happened to know is there were some Mujahedin who were there; you don't know if that was the El Mudjahedin Detachment or not or a different group perhaps? Would I be right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right. At that point in my statement, I clearly stated that we were at Livade. This member of theirs introduced himself as "Ajman." Was their command post there or not? I don't know. I didn't know at the time, and I can't be certain. As for Borovica I know that there was an element there. Was it the El Mujahid unit or not, I don't know, but there were foreigners there of Afro-Asian extraction. I can't say they were from the El Mudjahid Detachment or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you know there were Arabs of Afro-Asian extraction, but you don't know if they in fact belonged to the El Mujahid or a different group?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or a different group. I don't know, and to be quite frank, I didn't ask too many questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Were someone, for example, to believe that all the Arabs who ever came to Bosnian at the time were a compact, unified group, would that be true or accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on that, please?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "no," I'm not denying what you say. My evidence implies that you are right. All of the groups falling under the name "El Mujahid," and those were members of Afro-Asian origin, not just Arabs, that's why I'm using the expression "Afro-Asian origin" or "extraction," they were not a single entity, they were not an entity that was easy to coordinate, to work with, and to put it quite mildly, a unit that could have been placed under a unified system of command, so that's what I'm saying in response to your theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's still a little bit unclear. Let's try to clarify. Do you agree that not even the BH Army had exact information on who those Arabs were; were they a single group, were there five different groups, were there two groups, three? That's what I mean. They weren't all together under the El Mudjahedin Detachment, they were not a single group. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Excuse my interruption, but, Ms. Vidovic, do you want me to follow your cross-examination or not, simply because I can no longer follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I have a splitting headache, and I find it very difficult to focus right now. That may be why I'm speaking too fast. I will take that into account, by all means. Thank you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Right, Witness, let me ask you something else now. Can we please look at Exhibit 511. Witness, the translation has been marked as attachment 0185-5080. Page 20 of the Bosnian, please. Witness, you remember the Prosecutor showing you this document today?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you explained that this invitation was sent to the forward command post in Zenica, to the OKM in Zenica, and someone passed the information along to you. And now let me ask you this. It says: "Call for the commander by General Delic." I wish to clarify this. Did you know whether General Sead Delic was also actively involved in Operation Farz?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But it doesn't say here: "Call from General Rasim Delic" or what I would find natural: "Call from the commander of the Supreme Command Staff." That's not how it reads; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're entirely right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you can't rule out the possibility that this call may have come from General Sead Delic, can you?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I believe is that whoever passed this information along to me should have indicated this, whether the call had come from General Delic, the commander of the Supreme Staff Command, or from General Sead Delic, commander of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army. But let's clarify this straightaway. Had this been about something like that, I'm certain that General Sead Delic would not have gone through the basic command post of the 3rd Corps, because he was probably directly in touch with Mr. Mahmuljin about this. I'll refrain from further comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What if I were to put to you that General Delic, on the 13th of September, was nowhere near Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor could he have been in Visoko, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. Which General Delic, Madam Vidovic, now that we have introduced General Sead?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Rasim Delic, I mean General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was far away on the 13th of September. Would you accept the possibility that maybe this document is not clear about who called?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would accept that possibility. I didn't know at the time where General Rasim Delic was. For that reason, and I did comment a while ago, I would be embarrassed to make any assessment whatsoever for fear it might be erroneous. I know that Mr. Delic was in touch with Sakib Mahmuljin, commander of the 3rd Corps, but I have no idea where Mr. General Rasim Delic was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know for a fact that Sead Delic, for example, may have gone to Visoko, may have phoned the basic command post for any reason whatsoever. You can't rule that out, can you ?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't know. I can't rule it out, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify matters even further, did this person tell you that this was Commander Delic or did the person just say that this was General Delic?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote is what I heard, literally. This is the way the information was submitted to me, to the letter, and that's how it was recorded, who it came from, who it was being forwarded to, and my initials, as you can see. As I said a while ago, I would be embarrassed to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me ask you something. Could we put this document away, please. Let me ask you something on a different topic. You were asked a number of questions that directly or indirectly touch upon the issue of the prisoners of war in the summer of 1995, and I would like to ask you some questions about that. Mr. Mrkaljevic, do you agree that the treatment of prisoners of war in the BH Army was fully regulated by the rules of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct in what you say. I myself, when I was in contact with the prisoners of war, I always bore in mind the rights of the prisoners of war, to be treated in the spirit and the letter of the Geneva Conventions, and all BH Army personnel that I know who were in contact with the prisoners of war abided by that fully, in my belief, and I base that belief partly on my own personal attitudes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This is something that is quite important to me. The French interpretation that I received indicated "I believe" -- oh, yes, yes, now I see. I do apologise. Yes, it's fine now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please look at Exhibit 392, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkaljevic, do you agree with me that you have in front of you an order from the General Staff, dated the 8th of May, 1995? This is the order for the implementation of the provisions of International Law of War.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the right-hand side. Do you agree that this order was sent to the commands of all corps, that this is what it says here?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle of the document, among the addressees, I see that it says here the Kakanj command post, all corps commands, and then all the other units and commands that were in contact with the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the Geneva Conventions a little while ago. Do you agree that this document was received by the 3rd Corps and that all of you knew about this order about the treatment of the prisoners of war, that they should be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 2. That's on page 2 in the English version. Do you agree that access to prisoners is to be allowed for the Red Cross, that this is the order?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we look at paragraph 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the prisoners of war should not be quartered in areas caught up in immediate combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 5. Here it is ordered that the units of the BH Army should be informed about this order?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in the 3rd Corps and in all the units subordinate to the 3rd Corps were aware of this order and the fact that it was stipulated how the prisoners of war are to be treated?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally was aware of all that, and I believe that all of my colleagues who were in the 3rd Corps Command were quite aware of all this and that they complied with this in their acts and actions. This is an order that came from the highest level in the BH Army, and I believe that it was probably through this order -- or rather that all members of the BH Army were made aware of the contents of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to observe one little point. Could we please zoom in on the stamp. Sir, whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is General Rasim Delic's signature. That's his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What number stamp is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This stamp bears the number "3," and if you allow me, I can explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, in the Intelligence Department, if I had an order that was to be dispatched urgently to the lower-level units, this order was drafted as a document and it was sent to the General Affairs office. In the General Affairs office, a clerk would go through this document to check for any grammatical errors, and then this document would go to the commander for his signature. Let me make this even more clear. In this case, it would be the commander of the 3rd Corps. He would be signing this document. This is just an example. Once the document was signed, an indication would be made about the person who drafted the document. If I drafted the document, that was a lower-level service in the corps, then the stamp would bear the number "2" or "3". In this case, it was "3". If the order was made in the office of the commander, the stamp would have number 1. So this is the stamp that was under the control -- strict control of the senior officer in the Command. On the basis of what I was able to see, this document was drafted in the personnel section or in the legal unit of the personnel section, and it was then taken to General Delic for his signature. He signed it. And then in the General Affairs section, it was sent to the legal unit, and that's why it bears the stamp with the number "3". The document in this form is then sent to the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say General Rasim Delic will sign, he doesn't put his stamp on, the document goes back to the general legal administration office where it then gets stamped? Is that what you're saying, in short?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And when you see a stamp on a document, some stamps are designated "1", some "2", some "3". The stamp that bears number 1 is kept by the commander. The stamp with number 2 is usually used by the chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the unit in question. In this particular case, when we're talking about this document here, if we have a stamp with the number "1", that would be the commander, General Rasim Delic, the commander of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you see, when you tried to answer my question, you confused me because you made an example about a document drafted somewhere else or being done by somebody lower than General Rasim Delic. Now, this is a document signed by General Rasim Delic. It bears stamp number 3. I just want to know, because of what you said a little earlier, that stamp number 3 was used by personnel. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that document which bore stamp number 3 was signed for General Rasim Delic by somebody else. Now, this one is signed by General Rasim Delic himself, and I'm just saying: How does then stamp number 3 come onto this document if it was signed in General Delic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain a little while ago. I'm sorry if I failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do so very briefly, and don't give examples of other people drafting the document. This one is signed by General Delic. Just tell us about this one, if you know. If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a member of the army, I can explain this very briefly. The document was drafted by another service that is in charge of some legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to hold you there. Forget about the drafting. The document is before General Delic for signature. He signs. What then happens? It doesn't matter where it was drafted. Why doesn't he put the number 1 stamp then on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't explain that to you now, why he didn't put his own stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then can you explain, if he's there and he doesn't put his own stamp, how then this stamp comes on? Does it mean -- and let me just do it very quickly for you. Do you mean that he just signs and the person who brought the document takes the document back to his office, and in his office there's the number 3 stamp which he then puts? Is that the explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I wanted to understand. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me just ask you one question in order to clarify this for the Trial Chamber and for all of us, indeed. Do you agree that the commanders had their office, their cabinet, and that some documents were drafted in the office?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. That's precisely what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were also various services or administrations that also produced documents?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some of those documents, because of their importance, had to be signed by the commander?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once such a document is signed, it is always recorded in the originating unit, it bears the appropriate number, and that is why it is sent back to that particular unit or section where it is stamped?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. That's what I tried to explain. The unit or section drafting the document is responsible for certifying this document with a stamp and sending it to the lower-level units. That's what I was trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine, fine, thank you. At any rate, Your Honours, we will have witnesses who work there, and we will explain that through them. Witness, let us now go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He explained it when I asked him, really, even when you -- he's given the same explanation that he gave to me, so I'm happy with the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to look at document Exhibit 444.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, is this a document or exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as we wait for this document to show up, you remember that we were talking about the orders on the implementation of the International Law of War were sent to the lower-level units, and now I would like you to look at this document here. You see that this is a document from the 35th Division, bearing the date of the 18th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that this is an order for the continuation of the attack, Proljece-95 and -- witness, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please look at page 8 in the Bosnian version and page 21 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go away, is this an order from the 35th Division to the corps, to the 3rd Corps? The division is giving an order to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, that's not what I said. Maybe there is a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, I'm reading the document. It comes from the 35th Division. That's where it comes from; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is addressed to the 3rd Corps Command, and I'm asking the question: Do I understand that the division is giving an order to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I was asking the witness myself. That's why I'm looking at him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards this order, I would like to ask for a copy of this document or, rather, to move it to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the upper right-hand corner, there is a stamp, the 35th Division Command, stamp number 1. This order is sent to the 3rd Corps Command not so that they can execute this order, but it is sent to them for their approval. And if there is any need or any opportunity after this order is analysed, some corrections can be made, and then another order is drafted which will then include the instructions and corrections received from above. So this order is not sent to the Corps Command so that they can execute it, but for their revision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's a proposal of an order sent to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry to interrupt you, Madam Vidovic, but I just wanted to understand that little problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This has greatly assisted us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we please go to page 8 of the Bosnian. Twenty-one is the English page. Can you please look at item 4 -- 11.4, actually. My question to you is very brief. It's quite obvious that in the 35th Division, one knew about the orders concerning International Law of War. If you look at this: "Bring in all prisoners to the nearest unit's OV, then to the 35th Division OV Collection Centre in Zavidovici with the 35th Division Military Police Company," it is obvious that they are separating POWs from the area of combat operations by this order; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, madam. But if I may provide a brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Keep it brief, please.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time there's an order to commence and execute combat operations, it has a number of items, and this defines all those involved, staff commands and subordinate units. It says that they should stick to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions when dealing with POWs, and you can find this same instruction in all the orders that were produced. I'm not talking about 1995 and onwards, but the even earlier ones, orders issued by superiors to subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. If the witness could please now look at Exhibit 554, which is a document that he was shown earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness -- could we just zoom in slightly for the witness to see what it's about. You've been asked a great many questions about this document by both the OTP and the Chamber. What I'll ask you is to provide a number of clarifications. Could you please first look at the top of this document. This is a telegram; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Based on this, I infer that at this point in time no other communications systems were operational between you and this particular forward command post at Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "no," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no other communications system that was operational at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you exchanged telegrams; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The time at which this document was produced, the 24th of July, 1995. All right. I see that there was a forward command post of the 3rd Corps at Orahovo, and what I want to ask you is this: I'm right, aren't I, if I say that at this time, within the BH Army, there was a large-scale operation in progress in order to lift the blockade of Sarajevo, known as Action T; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. In my statement to the OTP, I pointed out that in order to carry this out, to carry out what follows, based on this report, the night before, on the 23rd, I stood up to my superior, Edin Husic, and I refused to carry out this order. I simply said "no." I was physically exhausted by this time because I had already spent 20-something days in the area around Sarajevo. I have certain photographs -- I have certain photographs back home showing me at the time. Someone might just be scared to death if they looked at me in those photographs. I had no time to rest, I had no time to eat or sleep or anything. I refused to carry out this order because the officer who was at this command post in Zenica at the time, who was supposed to implement this order, failed to do so. I don't know why. But after all, I eventually agreed, at the suggestion of other colleagues and the forward command post at Orahovo, as I said in my previous statement, the distance from Sarajevo is about 30 kilometres northeast. I got into my car and I drove to Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Orahovo is the forward command post of the 3rd Corps for that particular operation, Operation T?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Operation T, lifting the siege around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please, please, am I right if I say that General Mahmuljin, at the time, and most of his Command were at Orahovo?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, most of them were at Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd, he was. On the 24th, he came to Panorama Hotel for a briefing at about 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Panorama," that's in Zavidovici?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, are you trying to say that he came to Zavidovici?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he came to Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding is you're writing this document in order to inform General Mahmuljin because your direct superior, Edin Husic, is not around. Right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, precisely. I did say in my evidence previously that my role was, at the same time, to stand in for Mr. Edin Husic at certain times. However, at the basic command post in Zenica, Amir Abazovic was standing in for Commander Husic. He was a captain. And together with Ekrem Halihodzic, they were supposed to go to Zavidovici in order to try to deal with this problem that had just arisen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Let me ask you something else. Obviously, and it was just in Orahovo, how far is that from where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 90 kilometres, more perhaps. Perhaps 120, 130, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What remains unclear is this: You have instructions from General Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say, "My superior, Husic, gave me instructions to the effect that I should not work with POWs." Just a minute, sir, just a minute, please. What remains unclear to me, at least, is this: If Mr. Edin Husic is away, he's 90 kilometres away from you, that's one thing I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 120 kilometres away from me. The night before, when I cleared out on the 23rd, he immediately, and I mean immediately, made this suggestion to me. He immediately instructed me, "Don't get involved too much with POWs," the reason being a different service was tasked with dealing with that problem. "Your responsibility is to resolve the issue of the documents that were seized." Again, I pointed out that I refused this order, I refused to follow this order, I refused to carry it through, the reason being there was another officer who was in charge of this who simply failed to deal with it. Normally, to be quite honest, I was the one who was always appointed whenever there were chestnuts to be picked out of the fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic told you this on the 23rd, in the evening; right?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 23rd, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 23rd in the evening --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the speakers please be asked to not overlap. Thank you. It is becoming truly impossible to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreters are really having a rough time. They are complaining. Just read what they are saying, "Interpreters note," and I can say they are really saying, "Please." May I just add, Judge Lattanzi has also been saying that the French interpretation is much slower than the English interpretation, so if you interrupt in the English, it means that hers has hardly even begun.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please not barge in every time I finish my question. Leave some time between. Thank you. So what I was asking you about, you received instructions from Mr. Husic on the 23rd, the evening of the 23rd. That was my understanding. Now, can you tell me this: When exactly did you receive instructions from General Mahmuljin, or, rather, when did you receive what the document says, "Approved planned activities for the day, General Mahmuljin"; when?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mahmuljin, having received my report, the commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin, at 2200 hours that night, the night of the 24th of July, he approved these activities, meaning he approved these activities, but I was sort of sticking more to the instructions previously received by my direct superior, Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else. Be that as it may, you did not write or submit any sort of information to do with poor treatment, mistreatment, physical abuse, any sort of poor treatment of prisoners at all?

utterances.speaker: SEJFULAH MRKALJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I never submitted any information like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Mundis, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question about this aspect. You said, "I refused to carry out this order." There were two orders; right? There was one about you not getting involved with the prisoners, with the issue of prisoners. There was another order which said that you had to deal with the document issue. Therefore, you refused to carry out the order telling you to deal with the documents; right? Because you were too tired, that was my understanding. I'm not entirely clear about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry if you misunderstood my evidence or perhaps because it has been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably it was me misunderstanding your answer. At one point in time, you said you were told not to get involved with the prisoner issue; you were told to resolve the document issue. And then you said, "I refused to carry out that order." I'm not sure which one you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to explain what this is about, this misunderstanding. When I said that I refused to carry out an order, that was in reference to the order on my departure, the order telling me to leave Orahovo for Zavidovici. That's what my refusal was about. It was in reference to that particular order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks for clarifying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have one little question relating to the resubordination of the El Mujahid Detachment to the 35th Division, and my question is: Was your section given any information about the resubordination of the El Mujahid Detachment to the 35th Division? Were you notified of this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When resubordination is carried out, it's done by whichever unit is responsible for this resubordination. At the same time, all the services and departments at the 3rd Corps Command are familiarised with any order on resubordination. How, this is a matter for the Intelligence Department, and we need guidance in planning all activities of the resubordination or any particular instance of the resubordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, this is very interesting. I was not aware of that. Can you explain what steps you took to facilitate the resubordination of the El Mujahid Detachment to the 35th Division in, when was it, 1995, July 1995, I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm 100 per cent certain. This is a Bosnian proverb. That is why I said, "Excuse me, this is a Bosnian proverb." We would have done anything that we were asked to do just to make this situation about resubordination easier. However, when a superior officer drafts an order, this order normally details tasks and responsibilities. Based on the specific order, specifically the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps Command, had certain responsibilities. The question, the issue of resubordination itself, well, we didn't have any influence on that or responsibilities regarding that, not really, except for the following situation or possibility: Say there was a subordinate unit that was requesting new intelligence, fresh intelligence from us, upon their arrival in a new deployment area, that was the one exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if I have understood you correctly. Perhaps I should rephrase my question. Did you take any steps at all to further the resubordination of the El Mujahid Detachment to the 35th Division in the summer of 1995? Do you recall if you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the summer of 1995, the Intelligence Department of the 3rd Corps had the following responsibility: We made available to the 35th Division all of our new intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But did you have any intelligence on the El Mujahid Detachment which you passed on to the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think you misunderstand me. We don't provide intelligence on the El Mujahid Detachment. We provide intelligence on the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure I have misunderstood you, and maybe you have misunderstood my question. I was interested to know whether your unit was in any way involved in the resubordination of the Mujahid Detachment to the 35th Division, and the reason I'm asking, in order to clarify this for you, is that it has been surrounded with some degree of unclarity, during this trial, just how and why and when the Mujahid Detachment was resubordinated down to the 35th Division and back again to the 3rd Corps, and back again to the 35th Division. This, at least in my view, is obscure. So now that you are here and you are in the intelligence service, I wanted to know if you can help us out on that. If you can't, then that's fine. I wouldn't expect you to, but I couldn't help asking the question and taking the advantage of your being here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talking about the intelligence situation, intelligence on the El Mujahid Detachment, specifically, this sort of information could only have been provided by a different service, the Military Security Service, in as far as they had any intelligence on them at all. My own service dealt with issues regarding the enemy alone, any information, any data on the enemy that we retrieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so glad. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Any questions arising from the questions by the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good timing, sir. It's just the time to end your testimony, and it's time to break. Thank you very much for coming to testify. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I just wanted to say thank you and we wish you a pleasant journey back home. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Your Honours. It has been an honour for me to be of any assistance to you, and I certainly hope that I have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Court adjourned. We'll adjourn to tomorrow at 9.00, same courtroom.
